provenance.title: Adult malaria — recognition, severity and treatment prompts (Zimbabwe / sub-Saharan Africa)
provenance.primarySource: WHO Guidelines for malaria (2021); Zimbabwe Essential Medicines List (EDLIZ 2015) — antimalarial section
provenance.why: Malaria remains a leading cause of adult fever in Zimbabwe. Delay in recognising severe disease and in starting effective artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) costs lives. This pack surfaces the recognition prompts and referral thresholds an adult-medicine clinician needs at the point of assessment — it does not prescribe dosing tables or stock management.

sourceVerification.note: The WHO malaria guideline and EDLIZ are NOT vendored under docs/reference/who-dak/MANIFEST.json. Authored against published WHO 2021 guidance and EDLIZ first-line ACT (artemether-lumefantrine); ships ENGINEERING_SEED until primary texts are vendored and MOHCC ratifies national thresholds. RDT-first strategy and severe-malaria referral criteria follow WHO structure; exact transport and inpatient thresholds are national operational decisions.

rules.name: Fever in an endemic area — suspect malaria and test before treating
rules.message: Fever in a malaria-endemic area — suspect malaria and perform an RDT or microscopy before treating.
rules.explanation: In Zimbabwe and much of sub-Saharan Africa, malaria must be in the differential for any adult with fever. Treating on clinical grounds alone drives unnecessary antimalarial use and misses alternative diagnoses; withholding treatment while awaiting a test is unsafe when the pre-test probability is high.
rules.requiredAction: Perform a malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or thick/thin film microscopy now. Do not start ACT on fever alone without a positive test or documented severe-malaria criteria requiring parenteral treatment while awaiting confirmation.
sourceRefs: WHO Guidelines for malaria (2021) — test before treat

adaptation.whoStatement: All suspected malaria cases should be confirmed with a parasitological test before treatment where possible.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published; RDT-first is national policy.

testCases.name: fever in endemic area — suspect fires
fever but not endemic — gate excludes
no fever — rule does not apply

rules.name: Uncomplicated malaria confirmed — start ACT (EDLIZ first line)
rules.message: Uncomplicated malaria confirmed — start artemisinin-based combination therapy per national protocol.
rules.explanation: A positive RDT or blood film in an adult without severe features indicates uncomplicated malaria. EDLIZ lists artemether-lumefantrine as the first-line ACT for Plasmodium falciparum. Delay beyond 24 hours increases progression to severe disease.
rules.requiredAction: Start artemether-lumefantrine (or the ratified national ACT) at full adult dose for the weight band, complete the full course, and arrange review if vomiting prevents oral intake.
sourceRefs: WHO Guidelines for malaria (2021) — ACT for uncomplicated P. falciparum

adaptation.whoStatement: Artemisinin-based combination therapy is recommended for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria.
adaptation.nationalStatement: EDLIZ first line: artemether-lumefantrine pending ratification of any formulary update.

testCases.name: positive test without severe signs — ACT fires
positive with severe signs — severe rule owns this

rules.name: Severe malaria features — urgent referral / parenteral treatment
rules.message: Severe malaria suspected or confirmed — urgent referral for parenteral artesunate and inpatient care.
rules.explanation: Severe malaria — impaired consciousness, convulsions, respiratory distress, shock, acidosis, renal failure, severe anaemia, or inability to retain oral therapy — kills within hours. Oral ACT is insufficient; intravenous or intramuscular artesunate and supportive care are required at a facility that can manage complications.
rules.requiredAction: Arrange immediate transfer to the nearest facility capable of parenteral artesunate and critical care. Start pre-referral artesunate if national protocol allows and transfer is delayed. Treat hypoglycaemia, seizures and fever en route.
sourceRefs: WHO Guidelines for malaria (2021) — severe malaria

adaptation.whoStatement: Severe malaria is a medical emergency requiring parenteral artesunate and urgent referral.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published; referral destination and pre-referral dosing are national operational decisions.

testCases.name: severe signs present — urgent referral fires
no severe signs — does not fire
severe signs not assessed — must not fire

rules.name: Negative test but high clinical suspicion — repeat test and do not dismiss
rules.message: Malaria test negative but clinical suspicion remains high — repeat the test and review the diagnosis.
rules.explanation: RDTs and films can be falsely negative in early infection, partial treatment, or prozone effect. Dismissing malaria on a single negative test in a febrile patient from an endemic area has caused preventable deaths.
rules.requiredAction: Repeat RDT or microscopy in 12–24 hours if fever persists, and investigate alternative causes in parallel. Do not withhold retreatment if severe features develop.
sourceRefs: WHO Guidelines for malaria (2021) — repeat testing

adaptation.whoStatement: WHO recommends repeat testing when suspicion remains after a negative result.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Repeat-test prompt encoded for endemic adult fever where a single negative must not close the episode.
adaptation.rationale: Encodes an explicit repeat-test prompt for endemic adult fever so a single negative does not close the episode.

testCases.name: negative with high suspicion — repeat prompt fires
negative with low suspicion — does not fire

rules.name: Malaria in pregnancy — treat promptly with pregnancy-safe regimen
rules.message: Malaria in pregnancy — treat promptly with the pregnancy-safe antimalarial regimen.
rules.explanation: Malaria in pregnancy increases maternal anaemia, miscarriage, stillbirth and low birth weight. Some antimalarials are contraindicated in pregnancy; delay is as dangerous as the wrong drug.
rules.requiredAction: Start the ratified pregnancy-safe ACT or quinine regimen for the trimester. Refer if severe features or first trimester where national protocol requires specialist input. Arrange obstetric review and fetal surveillance.

adaptation.whoStatement: Pregnant women with malaria should receive prompt effective treatment with a pregnancy-appropriate regimen.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Exact regimen by trimester is a national ratification decision.

testCases.name: pregnant with positive test — caution fires
pregnant with negative test — does not fire
